facts.title: Named After the Thunder God
facts.text: Thorium was discovered in 1828 by the Swedish chemist Jons Jacob Berzelius, who isolated it from a black mineral sent to him from Norway. He named the new element after Thor, the Norse god of thunder, and named the mineral itself thorite. It was one of several elements Berzelius pioneered, alongside cerium and selenium.

facts.title: Radioactive Without Anyone Knowing
facts.text: For seventy years thorium was thought to be a perfectly ordinary metal, because radioactivity had not yet been discovered. In 1898 Marie Curie and, independently, Gerhard Carl Schmidt found that thorium emits radiation, making it one of the first elements ever recognized as radioactive. This work helped Curie coin the very term radioactivity.

facts.title: An Element That Glowed in Lamps
facts.text: From the 1890s into the 20th century, thorium dioxide was the key ingredient in the gas mantle, the little fabric mesh that made gas street lamps and camping lanterns shine brilliantly white. When heated in a flame, thoria glows intensely due to candoluminescence. Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach built an industrial empire on this invention.

facts.title: Almost Eternal Half-Life
facts.text: The main natural isotope, thorium-232, has a half-life of about 14 billion years, roughly the age of the universe itself. This means that nearly all the thorium present when Earth formed is still here today, having barely begun to decay. Its slow, steady decay is one of the main sources of the heat that keeps Earth's interior molten.

facts.title: More Abundant Than You'd Guess
facts.text: Thorium is about three to four times more common in Earth's crust than uranium, and roughly as abundant as lead. The richest deposits occur in the mineral monazite, mined from beach sands in India, Brazil, Australia, and the United States. A single tonne of ordinary granite contains enough thorium to hold meaningful amounts of energy.

facts.title: A Fuel That Isn't Quite Fuel
facts.text: Thorium-232 cannot directly sustain a chain reaction, but when it absorbs a neutron it transforms into uranium-233, which is an excellent nuclear fuel. This makes thorium a fertile material rather than a fissile one. Experimental molten-salt reactors, including one run at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the 1960s, were built to exploit exactly this conversion.

facts.title: One of the Densest Metals
facts.text: Pure thorium is a soft, silvery metal that is surprisingly dense, at about 11.7 grams per cubic centimetre, heavier than lead. It also has one of the highest melting points among the actinides, around 1750 degrees Celsius. Freshly cut, it is bright and ductile, but it slowly tarnishes to grey and then black in air.

facts.title: Pinpoint Beams for Surgeons
facts.text: Because thorium dioxide has an extremely high melting point and refractive index, it was once added to specialty optical glass for high-quality camera and scientific lenses. Thoriated tungsten is still used today in electrodes for TIG welding and in some vacuum tubes, where a trace of thorium dramatically improves electron emission. These uses rely on thorium's physical properties rather than its radioactivity.

facts.title: No Job in Living Things
facts.text: Thorium has no known biological role in any organism, and the human body neither needs nor uses it. When ingested, most thorium passes through, but a fraction can lodge in bone and the liver, where its radioactivity poses a long-term health risk. This is why a former medical contrast agent called Thorotrast, used for X-ray imaging in the early 20th century, was eventually abandoned.

facts.title: Forged in Colliding Stars
facts.text: Like gold and platinum, thorium is created in the cosmos through the rapid neutron-capture process, thought to occur in supernovae and in the violent mergers of neutron stars. Astronomers can even detect thorium's spectral lines in ancient stars and use its slow decay as a cosmic clock to estimate their ages. Finding thorium in a star is direct evidence of one of the universe's most extreme events.
